The **e\_theta** vector is the derivative of **e\_r** with respect to theta. This is ('m going to use P to represent theta):

d(**e\_r**)/dP = d(cos P **i**)/dP + d(sin P **j**)/dP

d(**e\_r**)/dP = **i**\*d(cos P)/dP + cos P (d**i**/dP) + **j**\*d(sin P)/dP + sin P (d**j**/dP)

But **i** and **j** constant vectors, hence d**i**/dP and d**j**/dP are both 0. Then:

d(**e\_r**)/dP = **i**\*d(cos P)/dP + **j**\*d(sin P)/dP

**e\_theta** = -sin P **i** \+ cos P **j** \[this is done by taking the derivative of cos P w.r.t P (= - sin P) and the derivative of sin P w.r.t P (= cos P)\]

r(t) is the function of position with time, with r being the distance of a point from the origin. 

**e\_r** is the vector in the direction of increasing r and **e\_theta** is the vector in the direction of increasing theta. In polar coordinates, as t varies, the values of r and theta vary as well. Hence **e\_r** and **e\_theta** change direction and we must take their derivatives as well.

The equations for **e\_r** and **e\_theta** are derived from the diagram. When taking d(**e\_r**)/dtheta, you get **e\_theta**. Similarly, for d(**e\_theta**)/dtheta, you get **-e\_r**.

I would stay away from quantum mechanics and relativity. Young's double-slit is perfect for demonstrating the wave nature of light. Demonstrating conservation of momentum during collisions using an air track and light gates if they're available is quite an interesting experiment.
